title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident describes a deliberate attempt to manipulate AI language models at the input stage rather than exploiting a flaw inside the models themselves. The operation produced a large volume of text designed to look like credible academic output, with the goal of embedding pro-Israel narratives into the corpora or citation patterns that AI chatbots draw on when answering questions. The failure mode this exposes is not a bug in a model but a vulnerability in how models treat surface legitimacy, a site that looks like a think tank, uses real sources, and publishes at scale can be treated by an AI system as a trustworthy source even when its funding and purpose are concealed.

The point of intervention where this could have been caught was outside the AI systems entirely, in due-diligence processes around source provenance. The operation was ultimately disclosed through a foreign-agent registration filing, not through any detection mechanism built into the AI products it was trying to influence. That means the AI systems involved had no internal means of distinguishing this content from genuine independent research.

What is not established is whether any specific AI chatbot did in fact cite or repeat narratives from the Hanover Institute, whether the operation achieved its intended effect on AI outputs, or whether any legal finding has been made about the conduct of the parties involved.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

Israeli government funding helped create a fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute that published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in just nine days. The site, which appears academic and uses legitimate sources, presents pro-Israel arguments on contentious topics including genocide allegations, war crimes, and starvation in Gaza. The operation was designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots to cite and repeat these pro-Israel narratives. The company Piro Inc filed the operation as a foreign agent with the US Justice Department, revealing it was financed through Israeli advertising agencies and European media companies.

The broader campaign cost tens of millions of dollars and involved multiple contractors, including former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale's firm. Despite these efforts, Israeli officials have expressed frustration that the expensive public diplomacy campaign failed to improve Israel's standing in American public opinion. Recent polling shows Americans increasingly sympathize with Palestinians, with support for Israel dropping significantly since 2022. Experts warn that AI manipulation tactics like these represent a new threat to information reliability, as chatbots may spread narratives without citing sources that could be fact-checked.
